Original Article
Determination of the biochemical 
methane potential of food waste 
after aerobic storage and aeration 
pretreatment
Bruna Patrícia de Oliveira, Center for Engineering, Modeling and Applied Social Sciences, Federal 
University of ABC (UFABC), Santo André, Brazil
William Gustavo Sganzerla , School of Food Engineering (FEA), University of Campinas (UNICAMP), 
São Paulo, Brazil
Patricia Léo, Laboratory of Industrial Biotechnology, Bionanomanufacturing Unit, Institute for 
Technological Research of São Paulo State, São Paulo, Brazil
Tânia Forster-Carneiro , School of Food Engineering (FEA), University of Campinas (UNICAMP), 
São Paulo, Brazil
Gilberto Martins, Center for Engineering, Modeling and Applied Social Sciences, Federal University of 
ABC (UFABC), Santo André, Brazil
Received May 25 2022; Revised June 21 2022; Accepted July 07 2022;
View online August 01, 2022 at Wiley Online Library (wileyonlinelibrary.com);
DOI: 10.1002/bbb.2414; Biofuels, Bioprod. Bioref. 16:1733–1743 (2022)
Abstract: Food waste represents a relevant fraction of municipal solid organic waste, and anaerobic 
digestion can be an eco-friendly alternative for sustainable management in a circular economy framework. 
One of the challenges to the implementation of anaerobic digestion is the availability of easily degradable 
compounds in the substrate, which can be solved by the application of pretreatment to increase methane 
production. In this study, the influence of aerobic storage time and forced continuous aeration pretreatment 
on the biochemical methane potential of food waste was evaluated. The results demonstrate an increase in 
the methane production concerning the total volatile solids (TVS) of food waste stored for 7 days (425 NmL 
CH4 g−1 TVS) compared with fresh samples without pretreatment (375 NmL CH4 g−1 TVS). The adoption of 
forced and continuous aeration pretreatment on food waste for 4 days produced 456 NmL CH4 g−1 TVS for 
the leachate, 1.22-fold higher than that for the food waste without storage. In conclusion, the application 
of aeration pretreatment previous to anaerobic digestion can be an alternative to increase the methane 
potential from food waste. © 2022 Society of Chemical Industry and John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
Key words: anaerobic digestion; biogas; bioenergy; VDI 4630; Buswell model; energy; 
circular economy

Introduction
N
owadays, it is estimated that about 33.3% of all food 
produced globally for human consumption is lost in 
the supply chain, including agricultural production, 
processing, distribution, consumption and postharvest 
activities, which is equivalent to 1.3 billion tonnes per year.1 
Therefore, there is a growing interest in the management 
of food waste, especially owing to the environmental 
problems caused by the improper disposal of solid waste.2 
Eco-friendly technologies for waste management have been 
studied as an alternative for bioenergy recovery, considering 
the circular economy concept.3,4 The circular economy is 
a conceptual model widely used in waste management, 
and organic wastes are feedstocks that are well suited to 
playing a role in sustainable development based on the 
bioeconomy.5,6 Moreover, the bioenergy recovered from 
organic wastes can be a substitute for fossil fuels, reducing 
environmental impacts and contributing to the energy matrix 
decarbonization.7,8
Anaerobic digestion (AD) technology allows the treatment 
of the organic fraction of municipal solid waste (OFMSW) 
and the production of methane-rich biogas and fertilizer 
for agricultural use.9,10 The large-scale implementation of 
AD of the OFMSW, of which food waste (FW) represents 
a significant part, is a challenge for dissemination of the 
technology, especially owing to the low biodegradation 
associated with the presence of lignocellulosic compounds 
in the solid phase.11,12 Regarding the process stability and 
efficiency, the use of FW as a substrate in AD reactors shows 
some problems associated with the accumulation of volatile 
fatty acids and the inhibition of methane production,13 
particularly in the start-up of batch garage-type reactors, 
where unbalanced conditions occur owing to the rapid 
degradation of easily degradable compounds.14
Hence, the pretreatment of the FW previous to AD is a 
significant factor in increasing methane production.15 The 
physicochemical pretreatment of FW has been conducted 
to increase hydrolysis and facilitate the subsequent 
methanization.16,17 Pretreatments with microwave, 
ultrasound, ozonization, mechanical fragmentation, thermal 
treatment and enzymatic hydrolysis are expensive for FW 
and decrease the energy potential of AD.18,19 One of the 
alternative pretreatments to AD is the simple storage of FW 
under appropriate aerobic conditions, which can make the 
biomass suitable for methanization.20 However, the influence 
of the storage period on the subsequent AD of food waste is 
still unclear.21 The pretreatments can provide higher biogas 
yields and faster establishment of methanogenic microbiota.22 
Another pretreatment identified as a facilitator for further 
methanization is continuous aeration treatment.23 Compared 
with various types of mechanical, thermal or chemical 
treatments, it efficiently reduces biodegradable compounds, 
improves the production of hydrolytic enzymes and has low 
energy consumption.24
The main advantages of incorporating aeration in hydrolytic-
acidogenic reactors are the solubilization of organic substrates 
and improvement of the hydrolysis phase, which represents 
a positive effect on the methanogenic phase.25 In the specific 
case of garage-type reactors, this can be even more important 
owing to the high concentration of solids in the substrate to 
be digested. Before AD, the aeration step can be common 
practice for the industrial treatment of OFMSW in garage-type 
reactors since it reduces the excess of organic acids that can 
negatively impact the anaerobic process.26 Considering the 
complex AD process, the stages of hydrolysis and acidogenesis 
are considered the limiting stages of methanogenesis, and 
pretreatment is crucial to increase the methane yield.27
The distinction is not clear in the literature between what 
short and long pre-treatment times would be conducted prior 
to the AD of FW. Therefore, this study evaluated the effect of 
two pretreatments on food waste: storage in aerobic conditions 
and forced aeration prior to AD. The biochemical potential of 
methane (BMP) was used to analyze the influence of storage 
time and aeration flow on the anaerobic digestion performance.
Material and methods
Substrate and inoculum
The food waste samples were collected at the restaurant of the 
Institute of Technological Research (São Paulo, SP, Brazil). The 
collected residues were fractionated sufficiently to perform 
the two degradation experiments. In total, 9 kg of FW were 
obtained after separating the sample from the leftover dishes 
through a coarse sieve, with about 0.9 kg of liquid discarded 
and 11.1 kg of preparation residues, consisting of 6.9 kg of 
melon rinds and 4.2 kg of cassava husks. The samples of 
400 g were prepared with 50% in mass of food preparation 
residues and 50% of the leftover dishes, the first of which were 
manually cut into sizes not exceeding 1 inch. The samples 
were stored at −20°C. The mesophilic inoculum was obtained 
from an Upflow anaerobic sludge blanket digestion reactor of 
a poultry slaughterhouse (Dacar Company, Tietê, SP, Brazil).
Study of food waste storage for 4 and 7 days
The samples were thawed and placed in 2 L amber glass 
bottles and suspended using Nylon fabric to separate the 
leachate from the solid phase. In this experiment, the 
pretreatment condition was static storage. The 2 L amber

glass bottles containing the suspended substrates were kept 
under ambient conditions in a styrofoam box to avoid sudden 
temperature changes during the storage periods of 4 and 
7 days. Two openings at the bottom of the sides and one at the 
top of the box were provided for natural ventilation. At the 
end of the storage period, the material suspended in the fabric 
was weighed, and the volume of the leachate was collected and 
measured. The material suspended on the Nylon fabric was 
then mixed with the leachate and homogenized in a blender. 
The homogenized samples were submitted for analysis of pH, 
total solid (TS), and total volatile solid (TVS) according to 
the American Public Health Association (APHA).28 After the 
storage steps (0, 4 and 7 days), homogenized samples for each 
storage period (4 and 7 days) and for the control (0 days) were 
subjected to the BMP test, which was monitored for 41 days 
under mesophilic conditions (37°C).
Study of the continuous aeration of food 
waste for 4 days
A new experiment, similar to the previous one, was 
conducted to evaluate the influence of continuous aeration 
for 4 days on the samples. The samples were thawed and 
placed in 2 L amber glass bottles and suspended in Nylon 
fabric in the same way as in the previous experiment. 
The bottles were also placed in a Styrofoam box, but in 
this experiment, a dry compressed air flux of 1.7 L min−1 
(equivalent to 36 L air g−1 TS day−1) was forced through the 
solid samples suspended in the bottles by injecting it below 
the Nylon fabric through a hose. The continuous aeration was 
maintained for 4 days, with a total aeration of 144 L air g−1 
TS. At the end of the aeration period, an apparent dryness of 
the material was observed. The suspended solid material was 
weighed, and the volume of the leachate in the 2 L bottles was 
measured. The leachate and the suspended material in the 
fabric were treated independently. For the homogenization of 
the suspended material, the content of the triplicate samples 
was collected, and 100 mL of distilled water was added for 
processing in a blender. Since the leachate was also partially 
dried, 100 mL of distilled water was added to each bottle of 
the triplicate sample to solubilize the material adhering to 
the bottles. Triplicate samples of the homogenized suspended 
material and leachate were subjected to analysis of pH, TS 
and TVS.28 After the forced aeration, the AD experiment was 
monitored under mesophilic conditions (37°C), using the 
same inoculum as used in the previous test.
The elemental analysis of the substrates used in the 
study was carried out in triplicate using the Flash EA 1112 
(Thermo Scientific) equipment. The samples analyzed were 
microcrystalline cellulose (used as a reference substrate 
for the BMP tests)29 and the substrates after 0 and 4 days 
(suspended solids and leachate). Knowledge of the substrate’s 
chemical composition is essential for calculating the quantity 
and composition of the biogas produced.30 Equations (1) 
and (2) present the Buswell model to estimate the theoretical 
methane production from the elemental composition:31

Biochemical methane potential
The BMP was performed on the Automatic Methane 
Potential Test System – AMPTS II (Bioprocess®) equipment 
according to the conditions of VDI 4630.32 The amount of 
inoculum in each reactor represented 1.5% (w/v) of the total 
reactor volume (500 mL), based on the TVS content. The 
substrate to inoculum ratio used was 0.5 based on the TVS 
content, and the resulting total solids in the reactor were 
5.2%. The useful volume of the reactor was 375 mL (75%). 
All of the tests were performed in triplicate. For the BMP of 
substrates of the storage study, the reactors were prepared 
with 220 g of inoculum, 153 g of distilled water and 19 g of 
the substrate (4 and 7 days of storage) or 24 g for the fresh 
substrate (control reactor). For the reference substrate, 4 g 
of microcrystalline cellulose was used.29 For the BMP of 
the aeration study, the reactors were prepared with 360 g of 
inoculum (the same inoculum used in the previous BMP test) 
and 70 mL for the leachate or 14 g for the suspended solid.
Results and discussion
BMP of food waste stored for 4 and 7 days

the inoculum and the substrate at the beginning of the 
experiment and after storage under aerobic conditions. The

results indicate that the fresh samples (0 days of storage) 
presented lower values of TS when compared with the treated 
residues, which can be explained by the evaporation and 
degradation during the storage period. The experiment did 
not show a major change in the composition of the residues 
in the characterization parameters from 4 days of storage to 
7 days of storage. At the end of the 4 days, a leachate amount of 
76 ± 5 mL was obtained, which represents 18.8%, considering 
the average mass of 403 ± 15 g used. Additionally, at the end of 
the 7 days, an amount of leachate of 89 ± 9 mL was obtained, 
representing 22.4%, of the average mass sample of 394 ± 3 g. 
The generation of leachate for 4 and 7 days was similar, 
although there was an increase of around 15% from 4 days 
to 7 days. Degueurce et al.33 evaluated a storage pretreatment 
for OFMSW and observed that the conversion from solid to 
leachate ranged from 15 to 27% for different substrates after 
2 weeks of storage, and the largest degraded portion (about 
15%) occurred in the first 3 days. In addition, during a period 
of 5–8 days of storage and considering substrates of different 
compositions, the percentage of solid matter converted to 
leachate was 17.5%,34 corroborating the present study.
The results of the TS and TVS of the inoculum and 
substrates were used as a basis for the BMP tests. Figure 1(a) 
shows the daily methane yield obtained for the fresh food 
waste (control) and after storage periods of 4 and 7 days. The 
maximum daily methane production for the substrates with 
different storage periods was obtained on the first day of 
the experiment. For the microcrystalline cellulose, used as a 
reference substrate, the maximum production occurred on 
the third and fifth days. Considering the first day, the fresh 
samples (FW/0 days) presented higher methane production, 
followed by the samples stored for 4 and 7 days. The results 
corroborate other studies, which demonstrated that the 
pretreatment period with aeration, either passively or through 
forced aeration, reduces the impact of a high initial load 
on AD, promoting more stable reactors.24 The average net 
cumulative specific methane production of food waste stored 
for 0, 4, and 7 days and the reference substrate (Fig. 1b) 
showed that a 7 day pretreatment caused an increase in the 
cumulative specific methane production.
The BMP tests were considered up to the point when 
the net methane production started to decrease (when the 
methane production of the inoculum alone was higher than 
the production of the substrate). For the microcrystalline 
cellulose, a BMP yield of 335 NmL CH4 g−1 TVS was obtained, 
representing more than 80% of the theoretical value (415 
NmL CH4 g−1 TVS). The yield obtained from the fresh food 
waste was 375.0 NmL CH4 g−1 TVS, while for the residue 
stored for 4 days it was 365.0 NmL CH4 g−1 TVS and for the 
residue stored for 7 days it was 425.0 NmL CH4 g−1 TVS. Thus, 
the accumulated production up to this point shows that the 
residue stored for 7 days presented a production 16% higher 
than that for the residue stored for 4 days. These results may 
indicate that the extension of the storage period contributed 
to the consumption of readily available acids, which can cause 
inhibition and also modify the structure of the material, thus 
contributing to a more stable process.
The BMP test of food waste stored for 4 days was lower than 
that of the fresh residue, while the residue stored for 7 days 
presented the maximum methane potential, although it took 
twice as long to reach that. This aspect must be considered 
for viability analyses of plants since, although the yield was

better with a longer storage time, the time spent to obtain 
this production was relevantly longer. Lu et al.35 performed 
a storage pretreatment under anoxic conditions, concluding 
that the best results in terms of stability were found with 
pretreatement periods of 5 and 7 days, with the methane 
yield ranging from 397 to 484 NmL CH4 g−1 TVSadded. This 
fact indicated that a storage time of around 1 week is an 
appropriate pretreatment before AD.33
BMP of food waste continuously aerated 
for 4 days
At the end of the 4 day aerating period, the leachate collected 
presented a volume of 20.5 ± 4.4 mL, approximately 5.3% 
of the average initial mass (388.2 ± 6.1 g). After continuous 
aeration for 4 days, 31.8% of the initial mass was lost by 
evaporation, giving the materials a dry appearance. To 
avoid this detrimental effect of reduced substrate moisture, 
which can impair metabolic activities, one possibility would 
be to humidify the air before aeration. Table 2 presents a 
characterization of the materials before and after aeration. 
The residue after aeration was more concentrated owing to 
evaporation and carbon loss, both in the solid and the liquid 
fractions. The mass balance after continuous aeration of 
food waste is presented in Table 3. It was observed that the 
pretreatment reduced the initial mass by 31.8%, and there was 
a reduction of 8.5% of TS and 8.3% of TVS. The production 
reduction was 7.9%.

Figure 2(a) shows the specific daily methane production 
rate in the BMP test of fresh FW, the reference substrate, 
suspended material and leachate after a continuous aeration 
period of 4 days. In general, the fresh FW presents a relevantly 
higher peak on day 1, probably owing to the availability of 
short-chain acids readily available for consumption. The 
reference substrate presented two defined peaks, associated 
with the possible presence and action of hydrognotrophic and 
later acetoclastic archea.25,36 The suspended material showed 
peak production on the first day and a subsequent decrease. 
On the fifth day, an increase in the activity presented the 
second-highest production rate. The leachate also presented 
a peak on the first day, followed by relative inactivity until 
the fifth day, when methane production restarted gradually 
to reach a second peak after 11 days of digestion. This fact 
may be due to the high load of dissolved volatile fatty acids. 
According to Charles et al.,36 the aerating experiments also 
showed two peaks in the methane production profile, the 
first peak referring to the gas produced by hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens. The second peak was attributed to acetoclastic 
methenogenics that provided a rapid acetate consumption. 
This consideration was evidenced by isotope screening, which 
made it possible to verify that during the first 2 days of the 
process, there was no conversion from acetate to methane but 
rather an accumulation of acetate.36
From the accumulated methane production (Fig. 2b), it 
was observed that pretreatment caused an increase in the 
net cumulative specific methane production. The methane 
production accumulated in the control reactor increased until 
the 14th day of digestion, and the highest production speed 
occurred in up to 5 days for fresh food waste. As expected, a 
large methane generation occurred on the first day, probably 
owing to the readily available acids. However, this availability 
of volatile fatty acids for consumption, especially in larger-
scale operating systems, where the inoculum to substrate 
ratio is not so high as in BMP tests, may cause acidification 
of the medium, with a great possibility of overload and risks 
to system collapse.14 Beyond this, Fig. 2 also shows that the 
aeration caused an initial reduction of accumulative methane 
(reduction of the first peak). These results can be explained 
by the presence of readily available compounds that were 
consumed in the aerobic process. The suspended material, 
besides presenting a slow increase in production rate at the 
beginning, also produced for fewer days when compared 
with the leachate, so one possibility is that the pretreatment 
has facilitated hydrolysis, and thus the easily degradable solid 
materials have been transferred to the liquid fraction, leaving 
only the most complex degradation materials.
According to Xu et al.,25 a microaeration rate 
corresponding to 258 L air kg−1 TS day−1 produced 0.27 L 
CH4 g−1 TVSadded. The FW was aerated at the rate of 387 L 
air kg−1 TS day−1 and produced 0.4 L CH4 g−1 TVSadded, 
where the residue without aeration produced 0.2 L CH4 g−1 
TVSadded. Despite the reported advantages of microaeration, 
residual oxygen in the acidogenic leach bed reactor can 
inhibit the activity of methane-producing bacteria and 
decrease the methane yield.

oxidation of readily available materials. However, the leachate 
showed a longer production than the solid fraction, reaching 
the second peak after 11 days (Fig. 2a). These results can be 
explained by the possibility that the aeration stage provided 
structural changes in some soluble compounds of more 
complex degradation, making it possible that after 11 days of 
AD they could be consumed in the process and more quickly.
The present study compared the experimental with the 
theoretical methane yield, calculated based on the elemental 
analysis. Table 4 shows the elemental analysis and ash content 
of the substrates used in the BMP test after continuous 
aeration pretreatement. In general, the C/N ratios were 102 
(microcrystalline cellulose), 14 (fresh food waste), 16 (4-day 
aerated suspended material) and 14 (4-day aerated leachate). 
According to Kondusamy and Kalamdhad,30 carbon acts as 
the energy source for microorganisms, and nitrogen plays 
a role in increasing the microbiota. The recommended 
C/N ratio for a continuous process is around 25–30, 
considering the need to meet the nutritional requirements of 
microorganisms compatible with their feeding rates. In the 
case of the batch BMP test, this is not necessarily true because 
there is an excess of microorganisms. Low C/N ratios may 
represent protein-rich substrates like meats, for example, in 
the case of food waste.34 The excess nitrogen in continuous 
reactors can be toxic to the microorganisms and inhibit the 
methanogenesis but in batch experiments of the BMP, where 
the substrate to inoculum ratio is low (< 0.5 in terms of TVS), 
this imbalance represents little danger of inhibition.

Concluding remarks and perspectives
According to the BMP results, a short period of aerobic 
storage (up to 7 days) and high aeration rates of food waste 
did not result in a loss of methane-producing potential. 
Still, it reduced the initial peak of methane production 
on the first day, which may cause a reletive reduction in 
the risk of inhibition in the start-up of batch reactors. The 
results showed that the storage and aeration production 
reached similar results. The storage took twice as long. This 
fact, considering the process aspect, is not interesting. The 
intense and continuous forced aeration applied for 4 days 
caused an 8.3% reduction in TVS, which may reduce the 
methane-producing potential. Still, it was compensated 
for by the higher degradability of both the suspended solid 
and the leachate. The reduction of the initial methane 
production peak and the extension of the production period 
are very important for avoiding methanogenic inhibition. 
Concerning aerobic storage, the longer the storage period 
is (up to 7 days), the greater is the attenuation of the initial 
methane production peak, which can be explained by 
the oxidation of the readily available substrates. Despite 
this initial reduction of methane production rate, the 
accumulated specific production is higher, although over 
a longer period. This fact has to be taken into account in 
the design of batch reactors, considering that to achieve 
the same accumulated production after storage, a longer 
digestion period will be necessary.

The proportions of residues for metabolization in AD 
processes must be evaluated and monitored. Standard 
conditions are only a reference for industrial applications 
since the amounts involved in substrates are much lower 
than the amount of inoculum when solid waste is used. Thus, 
treatment units should predict lower losses and not operate 
at maximum production conditions. Although the storage 
period has contributed to the lowering of the easily degradable 
organic load, as observed by the production results of the 
first day, the aeration is more effective. Another highlight is 
that although the storage (7 days) reached a production level 
close to that of the aerated substrate for 4 days, it took longer. 
Therefore, the aeration process is more interesting because it 
provides faster production, even when the aeration is carried 
out in excess, as in this case, causing losses of TVS.
Conclusion
This study evaluated the influence of aerobic storage time and 
forced continuous aeration pretreatment on the BMP of food 
waste. The results presented suggest that aerobic pretreatment 
can be used prior to AD to improve biodegradability of food 
waste and to prevent the inhibition of methanogenesis. For 
instance, the methane production of the FW stored for 7 days 
(425 NmL CH4 g−1 TVS) increased when compared with the 
fresh samples without pretreatment (375 NmL CH4 g−1 TVS). 
The adoption of forced and continuous aeration pretreatment 
of food waste for 4 days produced 456.20 NmL CH4 g−1 TVS 
for leachate, 1.22-fold higher than that for the food waste 
without storage. Specifically, in large-scale garage-type systems, 
introducing aeration as a pretreatment can promote the 
reduction of the excess available organic load in the start-up 
of the reactors, which otherwise can acidify the reactor owing 
to the high substrate to inoculum ratio and negative impact 
on methanogenesis. In conclusion, the application of aeration 
pretreatment prior to anaerobic digestion can be an alternative 
to increase the methane potential from food waste.
